Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What is the primary focus of the Team Project?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Learning how to apply the resources of a team - the collective wisdom and expertise of about 35 people - against a project.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What was the Team Project formerly called, and why was it renamed?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: The Mini Systems Project - renamed to emphasise that the point is the team, not just a smaller systems exercise.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: How large is a Team Project team, and how long is the project?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: About 35 people, and about eight hours.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: Is the Team Project problem chosen or assigned?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Assigned - the brief is revealed on the Friday before the project week.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: Name three goals of the Team Project.
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Test-driving systems thinking concepts on a real wicked problem; appreciating how to structure and operate high-performing teams; and optimising team approaches, roles and personalities to prepare for the Systems Project.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What carries over from the 303 double diamond?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: The structure of a problem space and a solution space.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What changes about the double diamond in 403?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: The problem is assigned rather than chosen, the problem space is far more complex, the stakeholders are much more complex, and understanding the problem matters even more.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: Where do 303 and 403 sit on the Head matrix?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: 303 sits in the tame corner with clear problems and constrained solutions; 403 sits in the very wicked corner.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: Why is intervention a better word than solution?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Because you are very unlikely to solve a wicked problem - you can only influence or shift it in an attempt to have a positive impact.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What does slide 12 warn about systems thinking tools?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Tools, not a pathway to a specific solution - they are not computational, they help you understand the situation and contemplate choices, but they will not give you the answer.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: Is there a correct way to structure a 35-person team?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: No - most years no two teams are the same.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: Give one example team structure from a past cohort.
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: A strategic case group, an economic case group, and an editorial team doing the writing, proofreading and diagrams.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: Give a second example team structure.
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Sub-team leaders over team members, with editors embedded in each sub-team - or a split by research, editing and quality control.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What is the counter-intuitive difficulty of a 35-person team?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Having too much resource - the challenge is dividing work so everyone's expertise and bandwidth is used rather than relying on a handful of people.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: When should a team settle its structure?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: On the Thursday session, before the brief is released, so no time is lost once the project starts.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What habit from smaller projects breaks at Team Project scale?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Doing the work and managing the work at the same time - managing a large group is itself a substantial body of work.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What was the all-nighter failure story?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: A team leader rewrote work himself and stayed up all night, when he should have leveraged the team and put editing processes in place.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: Does the doing-versus-managing point apply only to the overall leader?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: No - even a sub-team leader may have so much coordination work that they contribute little personally to the detail.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: Name four kinds of team drama the lecturer anticipates.
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Disputes over who does how much work, someone getting bogged down, someone becoming unwell, and someone who believes they should be leading but did not get the role.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What does the lecturer say about the imperfection of team output?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Everyone has to contribute to something that will be inherently imperfect, and that will be true for the rest of your life.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What is the purpose of the team charters done in 204 and 303?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: To prepare you for this point, by having already determined how the team will handle conflict and manage projects.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: How does shared understanding of the problem change at 35 people?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: A subset of the team develops the understanding and communicates it, so most members have limited input into how the problem was framed.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What are you told to do if you disagree with how teammates framed the problem?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Run from what you are given - there is not enough time to relitigate it, and you must take as a given that teammates have done good work.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What is a lockdown point?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: An agreed date or time after which a piece of work is not changed any further, so the next stage can start from a fixed input.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: Why are lockdown points necessary?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Because the work is sequential and there is very little time, so handoffs need a fixed moment to close.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: Name the five points of the discovery and understanding slide.
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Understanding the problem and its systems is vital to problem statements; remember the 303 basics; it is still double diamonds at grand scale; do not overcomplicate or mix the problem and solution spaces; and decide who will understand the problem and how it will be shared.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What is the named over-complication risk in discovery?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Blurring the problem and solution spaces - people start merging things instead of carving out the problem space before considering solutions.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What must a team work out about ideation?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Which part of the team is actually involved in the solution diamond - it may not be everyone.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: Is systems research hypothesis oriented?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: No - scholarly research is hypothesis oriented; systems research is forecast oriented.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What resources does systems research draw on, compared with scholarly research?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Published literature from the past plus projections of future trends, whereas scholarly research uses published literature alone.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What are the findings of systems research used for?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Decision making and setting strategies, rather than advances in the field and future research.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: How is systems research shared?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Internally and with the client, rather than through publications and conference presentations.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What standard applies to rigour in systems research?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: The information and analysis must be valid, rather than the methodology being validated scientifically.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: Define systems research.
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: A systematic approach to collect data and analyse the information to uncover the interconnected aspects of wicked problems, manage stakeholders with conflicting requirements, and explore existing and potential solutions - ultimately to arrive at informed recommendations.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: Give four questions systems research actually asks.
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: How is this regulated by a government department, what industries are impacted, how do those industries operate, how many jobs do they have, and what exports do they have.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: Give the one-line contrast between systems and scholarly research.
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Systems research asks how the world is arranged; scholarly research asks what is true.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What is the policy on AI tools for the Team Project?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: They may be used but must be disclosed, within the policies outlined on Canvas.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What is a cluster map for?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Identifying the key components that make up a system and all the relationships inherent within it - the key part being drawing the connections between them.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What is an interconnected circle map for?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Deep exploration of relationships and cause and effect in system dynamics, within a refined area identified through the cluster map.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: How do cluster maps and circle maps relate?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: The cluster map is divergent, covering the whole system; the circle map is convergent, going deep on one region.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What does the lecturer say about how systems maps should look?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: The messier the better at the beginning - a big piece of paper on the wall with everyone contributing; a clean version can be recreated for the deliverable or put in an appendix.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What does the non-standard exemplar diagram demonstrate?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: That a team integrated mind mapping with causal loops in a way that was not standard, and did extremely well - so the tools should not be treated as absolutes.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What is mind mapping recommended for?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: As a starting point for the group's work, because it is a good way to understand a problem.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: Name the five steps of options assessment.
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Create a long list including the crazy options; group similar options and evaluate with CSF and DFV; consider the assessment scale you will use; evolve to a short list; and consider option packages.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What are options evaluated against?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: The DFV criteria, the critical success factors, and the problem statements.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What is a package of solutions?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: A combination of parts of separate interventions, each addressing a different problem statement, brought together as one recommendation.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: How does a package differ from a 303 solution?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: In 303 you choose one path forward and run with it; a systems project may need several partial interventions combined.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: Why do robust systems resist change?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Because of resilience, self-organisation and hierarchy.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What is the mistake people make when calling a system broken?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Assuming it is broken for everyone - a persistent system has accumulated over time and works for at least some of its stakeholders.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: Give the hospital example of a system that works for someone.
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Emergency departments are consistently over capacity, but the system has built up over time and some stakeholder groups are happy with the outcomes - the patients not among them.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: Which L9 canvas question does why-systems-work answer?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Does anyone benefit from the problem as a problem.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: Why does every systems challenge have a policy element?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Because these are problems that impact government as well as business and society, so the recommendation must navigate the machinery of government.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What made the Harbour Bridge decision an example of a wicked problem?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: The transport minister described it as a 50 to 100 year decision and the largest infrastructure investment in the country's history, affecting the economy, commuting and national values.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What sections does the Team Project deliverable contain?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: An executive summary, the strategic case, the economic case, an appendix, and references.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What is in the strategic case of the Team Project deliverable?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Project background, problem space, stakeholder analysis and requirements, and key assumptions.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What is in the economic case of the Team Project deliverable?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Long-list option assessment, recommendations of the short-listed options, and a summary of the proposed solution.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: Which business cases does the Team Project deliverable NOT include?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: The financial and management cases - the Team Project covers only the strategic and economic cases.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What belongs in the Team Project appendix?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: The requirements of key stakeholders by category, and the detailed assessment of long-list options.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: Roughly how long was the exemplar Team Project deliverable?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: About twelve pages.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What was the America's Cup team project brief?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: How to bring the America's Cup back to New Zealand, after it was defended in Spain and then Italy because it did not make economic sense to defend it here.

Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 13?: What was last year's team project topic?
Peter Rachor, who also taught ENGGEN 303: Addressing the invasion of exotic caulerpa.
